critical_concepts.elaboration: Organisms like plants that produce their own food, usually through photosynthesis. They form the base of the food web.
Ecological phenomenon triggered by the addition or removal of top predators and involving reciprocal changes in the relative populations of predator and prey.

interactive_questions.title: Ecosystem Balance Simulation
interactive_questions.prompt: A stable ecosystem requires a delicate balance between producers, herbivores, and carnivores. Too many predators or too few producers can lead to a collapse.
interactive_questions.question: Adjust the populations to create a stable ecosystem that runs for 10 generations.
interactive_questions.explanation: You've found a stable balance! This demonstrates that a much larger biomass of producers is needed to support a smaller biomass of herbivores.

theory.title: Population Dynamics
theory.content:
Ecosystems rely on a balance between Producers (plants), Primary Consumers (herbivores), and Secondary Consumers (carnivores).

Populations fluctuate in cycles. If prey increases, predators eventually increase. As predators increase, prey decreases, which then causes predators to decrease, allowing prey to recover.
theory.analogy: Think of a bank account. Producers are your income (deposits). Herbivores are your daily expenses (withdrawals). If expenses consistently exceed income, the account goes bankrupt (ecosystem collapse).
theory.application: In Yellowstone National Park, the reintroduction of wolves (top predators) controlled the elk population, which allowed willow trees to recover, eventually changing the flow of the rivers (Trophic Cascade).

interactive_questions.title: Energy Pyramid
interactive_questions.prompt: The flow of energy in an ecosystem can be visualized as a pyramid. Each level up has significantly less energy than the one below it.
interactive_questions.question: Build the energy pyramid from the bottom up.
interactive_questions.explanation: Correct! Producers form the base, followed by primary consumers, then secondary consumers. Only about 10% of energy is transferred up.

theory.title: The 10% Rule
theory.content:
In an ecosystem, energy is lost as heat at each step of the food chain. Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next.

  • Producers: 100% Energy
  • Primary Consumers: 10% Energy
  • Secondary Consumers: 1% Energy
theory.analogy: Imagine a pyramid of champagne glasses. You pour a whole bottle into the top glass (sunlight energy to producers), but due to spilling and splashing (metabolic heat loss), only a sip makes it to the glasses at the very bottom.
theory.application: This explains why apex predators (like tigers or eagles) are rare compared to plants or insects. An ecosystem simply cannot support a large number of top-tier consumers due to energy inefficiency.
